- Every pause card carries a real action (CARDFIX-1): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: Paused scheduled jobs are no longer dead ends: every pause/setup message now arrives with working buttons on Slack, Telegram, Discord and Teams. A job paused for a blocked shell command offers 'Allow once for this run' — one more run that asks live for that exact command, nothing permanently granted — and 'Pause job', which now really pauses the job from the card on every provider (it used to be guidance text). Double taps, crashed taps and concurrent taps all collapse into exactly one extra run.
- One permission surface, family-wide grants (CARDSIMPLE-1): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: Allowing a command once now settles its whole family: approve curl for one URL and future runs of curl with any arguments proceed without asking, on every lane that mints permission rules. Piped commands still never get an Allow button, dangerous variants inside an allowed family still ask (and only for that one run), and scripts or environment-dependent paths can never become broad grants. Exact rules and capability grants behave exactly as before — the only visible change is fewer permission prompts.
- Channel dispatchers: flatten repeated guards and split the Telegram callback by action kind (CHAN-2): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: The provider adapters are easier to read and change safely. Five repeated guards (Telegram, Slack, Discord, Teams) are computed once instead of per branch, and the Telegram callback — previously one ~700-line function handling every button tap — is now a thin dispatcher that builds one context object and hands each kind of tap (question answers, stop, job-permission card, memory/brain reviews, observer, retry, classic permission prompt) to a named handler in its own module. Nothing changed in behaviour: every existing test passes untouched. Complexity: dispatcher 11, largest handler 16 (ceilings 15/25).
- Job runner: split runActiveJob and runQuery by phase (CHAN-3): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: The two biggest functions in the runtime are now readable one phase at a time. The job run loop (runActiveJob, 733 lines in one body) and the SDK query loop (runQuery, ~600 lines) each became a short sequencer over one context object, with every phase a named function in sibling modules — setup/lease/agent/finalization for jobs, options/setup and one handler per message kind for the query loop. Nothing changed in behaviour: every existing unit and Postgres integration test passes untouched. Complexity on the AST counter: sequencers under 15, largest phase under 25 (ceilings 15/25).
- Agents can use what they are granted (GRANTED-1): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: Finished before the move to the new Forge.
- Chat-parity permissions for scheduled jobs (JOBPERM-1): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: Scheduled jobs now ask for permission the same way a chat does: when a job needs a tool it is not yet allowed to use, one living card appears in the job's chat with Allow/Deny buttons and no timer, the run waits in place, and an Allow-always answer is remembered for future runs. The job notification was rebuilt alongside it: exactly one message per run, edited from Running into the result, rendered natively on Telegram, Slack and Discord, leading with a one-line outcome, then the per-tool results, then the next run time. Operators also got a heredoc-aware command gate, honest 'this request stays open' wording on job prompts, and the KnackLabs incident class (one card edited ten thousand times) is closed by JSONB-faithful settlement.
- Settled job permission cards disappear like chat prompts (JOBPERM-3): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: Answered job permission cards now behave like chat prompts. When every request on a card is allowed, the card is deleted on Telegram, Slack and Discord (with a short approved receipt if the delete fails), and on Teams it becomes a one-line receipt card with no buttons. Requests that expired show as 'Expired: <command>' lines instead of lingering buttons; a denied request still keeps its live card row with one-tap Reconsider, as decision 0144 requires. The shared card record carries the retire outcome and the delete/receipt markers, so a retried delivery never deletes or edits twice and a recorded marker can never be rewritten. The Postgres once-card test now runs like a live job (delivered card, scheduler slot held), which is what exposed the ordering bug behind the earlier hang.
- Remove the providerConnection dual-read (LEGACY-2): its approval on main carries over, and it is finished: every part was done before the move. Outcome: The old providerConnection name no longer lives anywhere in the runtime settings path: the in-memory shadow field and its parser fill are gone, every providerAccount ?? providerConnection read now reads provider accounts only, writers stop creating the property, and the 19 expired architecture exceptions are deleted, so npm run check:architecture is green on main again. Behaviour is unchanged: a settings document that still says provider_connection keeps being rejected by the existing strict key check (now covered by a test), and the Slack approver lookup stays account-qualified. providerConnectionId and the missing_provider_connection enum are deliberately left alone (deferral D-0070).
